courseTitle: Incident Response, Threat Hunting & SOC Capstone

lessons.title: The NIST Incident Response Lifecycle

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the four NIST SP 800-61 phases from memory in order, then apply them to a new scenario of your own choosing (not the lesson's compromised-workstation walkthrough) — a phishing email that leads to a mailbox takeover — identifying one concrete action that would happen in each of the four phases.
slots.deliverable: A written four-phase breakdown (Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, Post-Incident Activity) applied to your own phishing scenario, with one concrete action named per phase.

lessons.title: Preparation: The Phase That Happens Before Anything Goes Wrong

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's three Preparation categories (written plan, trained team, ready tools/access), audit a hypothetical SOC's readiness against an 'isolate a compromised server' scenario and identify, for each category, one specific thing that must already exist before the first alert fires, following the lesson's departed-employee admin-access example.
slots.deliverable: A written three-category Preparation readiness checklist (plan, team, tools/access) for the isolate-a-compromised-server scenario.

lessons.title: Detection and Analysis: Confirming a Real Incident

slots.practicalActivity: Take the lesson's single-user-account alert scenario and write out, step by step, what Detection & Analysis has to establish before the team can move into Containment — distinguishing 'confirming this is real' from 'understanding its nature' — then name one incident type (ransomware vs. a quiet single account compromise vs. a reported-before-click phishing email) that would call for a very different containment response.
slots.deliverable: Your written two-part analysis (confirmation vs. nature) plus the three contrasted incident-type examples and their differing containment implications.

lessons.title: Containment, Eradication, and Recovery: Overview

slots.practicalActivity: Walk the lesson's compromised-workstation example forward as if the team skipped straight from alert to Recovery without Containment or Eradication — write out specifically what would go wrong at each skipped step, using the lesson's own sequence-dependency reasoning.
slots.deliverable: A written failure-mode walkthrough showing what breaks when Containment and Eradication are skipped before Recovery, referencing the lesson's sequence-dependency argument.

lessons.title: What a Real Incident Response Plan Contains

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's six core IR plan components (scope/objectives, severity classification, communication plan, escalation paths, tool/access inventory, legal/regulatory notification requirements), draft a one-page SEV1–SEV4 severity classification table with concrete criteria for each level, modeled on the lesson's ransomware-at-2-a.m. example.
slots.deliverable: A written SEV1–SEV4 severity classification table with concrete criteria, plus one worked example (your own incident type) showing which severity it would hit and why.

lessons.title: Incident Response Playbooks for Common Scenarios

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own three-step playbook outline for one scenario type not covered in the lesson's four examples (ransomware, BEC, data exfiltration, insider threat) — for example a DDoS attack or a lost/stolen laptop — modeling it on the lesson's ransomware playbook's level of specificity (isolate without powering off, check against known indicators, verify backups before assuming).
slots.deliverable: A written three-step playbook for your chosen scenario type, matching the specificity level of the lesson's ransomware playbook example.

lessons.title: IR Team Roles and RACI

slots.practicalActivity: Build a RACI matrix for three decisions (take a production system offline, approve a ransom-related communication, disable a user account), naming who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for each, following the lesson's 'take a production system offline' worked example and its one-Accountable-person rule.
slots.deliverable: A written RACI matrix covering three IR decisions with exactly one Accountable name per decision.

lessons.title: Tabletop Exercises: Testing the Plan Before You Need It

slots.practicalActivity: Design your own tabletop scenario with an opening scenario and three injects (new pieces of information), modeled on the lesson's Friday-at-5-p.m. ransomware example, then write out what gap each inject is designed to expose in a hypothetical team's plan, playbooks, or RACI matrix.
slots.deliverable: A written tabletop exercise script (opening scenario plus three injects) with the specific gap each inject is designed to surface.

lessons.title: Triage at Incident Scale, Not Just Single Alerts

slots.practicalActivity: Starting from the lesson's 'impossible travel' alert, write out the entity-based pull plan (in plain English) you'd use to gather every other alert and raw event tied to the same user account within the incident window, and list at least three categories of related events you'd expect to find, following the lesson's mailbox-rule / OAuth-grant / file-download example.
slots.deliverable: A written entity-based pull plan for the impossible-travel account, naming at least three related-event categories to search for.

lessons.title: Timeline Reconstruction from Multiple Log Sources

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's four-source example (email security, identity, endpoint, endpoint again) but with your own invented timestamps, build a normalized chronological timeline table and label each entry with its attack-chain stage (initial access, lateral movement, data staging), practicing the timestamp-normalization step the lesson flags as critical.
slots.deliverable: A written four-row chronological timeline table with normalized timestamps and attack-chain-stage labels for each entry.

lessons.title: Scoping an Incident: What Else Is Affected

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's three scoping checks (other accounts, other hosts, exfiltrated data), write out the specific check you'd run for each one against the previous lesson's compromised account, and explain what it would mean for the incident if the 'other accounts' check turned up a second SSO sign-in nobody had flagged yet.
slots.deliverable: A written three-check scoping plan (accounts, hosts, exfiltration) plus your explanation of the second-foothold risk if the accounts check surfaces a new sign-in.

lessons.title: Incident Severity Classification in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's four severity factors (business impact, data sensitivity, scope/spread, regulatory implications), classify two incidents sharing the same technical attack chain as the lesson's example but with swapped details: one hitting a marketing intern's account with access to nothing sensitive, and one hitting an HR director's account with access to employee SSNs — write the severity level and reasoning for each.
slots.deliverable: Your written severity classification and four-factor reasoning for both the marketing-intern and HR-director scenarios, showing why they land differently.

lessons.title: Short-Term vs. Long-Term Containment

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's compromised web server example, write out the specific short-term action and the specific long-term action separately, then describe what 'residual risk' looks like three weeks later if only the short-term action is ever done, following the lesson's own forgotten-isolated-host warning.
slots.deliverable: A written short-term/long-term containment breakdown for the web server scenario plus your description of the residual-risk failure mode.

lessons.title: Isolation Decisions and Their Real Tradeoffs

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's four decision factors (confidence, spread risk, business impact, reversibility) plus the compensating-control option, write out the isolation decision for a scenario of your own choosing where isolating a critical system would cause real business harm, and name who in a RACI structure should actually make that call.
slots.deliverable: Your written four-factor isolation decision analysis for your chosen critical-system scenario, naming the authorized decision-maker per the RACI structure.

lessons.title: Containing a Compromised Account vs. a Compromised Host

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's phishing-link-to-malware-to-cloud-mailbox example, write out specifically what is left exposed if the SOC performs only account containment, and separately what is left exposed if it performs only host containment, demonstrating why both are needed together, not sequentially.
slots.deliverable: Your written two-part exposure analysis showing what's left active after account-only containment and after host-only containment.

lessons.title: Preserving Evidence While You Contain

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's healthcare breach example, write out the correct order of operations (isolate, then acquire evidence, then eradicate) for a scenario where a server holding customer payment data may have been accessed, naming what specifically would be lost if the team powered off the server instead of isolating it.
slots.deliverable: Your written order-of-operations plan for the payment-data scenario, naming the specific evidence lost by powering off instead of isolating.

lessons.title: Eradication: Removing the Actual Root Cause

slots.practicalActivity: Using Meridian Outpatient Billing's scenario, write the PowerShell confirm-then-remove commands (modeled on the lesson's Get-ScheduledTask/Unregister-ScheduledTask, Get-LocalUser/Remove-LocalUser, and Get-ItemProperty/Remove-ItemProperty pairs) you would run against a fourth, newly-discovered persistence mechanism of your choosing, and name which Windows Event IDs (4720, 4698) you would cross-check tenant-wide to rule out a fifth.
slots.deliverable: Your written PowerShell confirm-then-remove commands for your chosen fourth persistence mechanism, plus your Event ID cross-check plan.

lessons.title: Restoring from Clean Backups the Right Way

slots.practicalActivity: Given a new confirmed-compromise timestamp of 6:15 AM Wednesday and a nightly backup job that runs at 1:00 AM, determine which backup (Wednesday 1 AM or Tuesday 1 AM) is safe to restore from using the lesson's timeline-based rule, then write out the additional checks (isolated-environment EDR scan, checksum integrity, backup-service-account compromise check) you'd still run before trusting it.
slots.deliverable: Your written backup-selection decision for the new timestamp scenario plus the full verification checklist you'd still run before trusting it.

lessons.title: Validation Before Returning to Production

slots.practicalActivity: Using Meridian's Remote Desktop Gateway and billing database server, write out the four validation checks (patch confirmation, persistence re-check, targeted vulnerability scan, monitoring window) as a literal pre-production checklist with pass/fail criteria for each line, and explain why 'the restore looked clean' is not an acceptable substitute for any one of the four.
slots.deliverable: Your written four-item validation checklist with pass/fail criteria, plus your explanation of why none can be substituted with a gut-feel judgment.

lessons.title: Phased Recovery and Monitoring for Reinfection

slots.practicalActivity: Using Meridian's three-tier recovery structure, design your own tiering plan for a 50-server environment with different criticality levels, naming what goes in Tier 1, 2, and 3 and which of the lesson's four reinfection signals (new outbound connections, recurring IOCs, exposed-credential logins, unusual log volume) you'd watch for before approving each tier's move to the next.
slots.deliverable: Your written three-tier recovery plan for the 50-server scenario, with the specific reinfection signal you'd watch at each tier gate.

lessons.title: The Lessons Learned Meeting

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's business email compromise example as a model, write your own lessons-learned meeting notes for the Meridian ransomware case from the Eradication & Recovery chapter, answering the three required questions (what worked, what didn't, what should change) with at least one concrete finding for each.
slots.deliverable: Your written lessons-learned meeting notes covering the three required questions for the Meridian-style incident, with at least one concrete finding per question.

lessons.title: Writing a Real After-Action Report

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's six AAR sections, write a full after-action report for the Meridian ransomware incident, including at least two action items that each name a specific owner, a specific deadline, and a specific checkable outcome, matching the 'Jordan configures MFA-status API access by the 15th' standard of specificity.
slots.deliverable: A written six-section after-action report for the Meridian incident with at least two fully specific, owned, dated action items.

lessons.title: Feeding New Detections Back into Sentinel

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's two-step KQL narrowing process, write your own detection rule for a different root cause of your choosing (e.g. a rogue local account creation pattern), starting from a too-broad first-pass query and narrowing it with a has_any condition the way the lesson narrowed schtasks.exe activity to AppData/Temp paths.
slots.deliverable: Your written two-step KQL query (broad first pass, then narrowed) for your chosen root cause, plus the entity-mapping fields you'd set for the resulting rule.

lessons.title: Measuring Whether the Response Actually Improved

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's three-incident MTTD/MTTR trend example, invent a fourth business-email-compromise incident's numbers that would either continue or break the downward trend, and write out what that result would tell the team about whether the fixes are still working, plus the two action-item completion checks (did Jordan grant access, did Priya's playbook change land) you'd verify.
slots.deliverable: Your written fourth-incident MTTD/MTTR data point with your interpretation of the trend, plus your two-item action-item completion check.

lessons.title: Hypothesis-Driven Threat Hunting

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own specific, testable hunting hypothesis for a LOLBin other than rundll32.exe (certutil.exe or mshta.exe), naming the specific binary, the specific suspicious behavior, and the specific log field you'd query, following the lesson's standard for what separates a real hypothesis from a vague feeling.
slots.deliverable: Your written testable hypothesis for a second LOLBin, naming the binary, behavior, and queryable field.

lessons.title: The Threat Hunting Loop in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: Run your previous lesson's LOLBin hypothesis through all four stages of the loop (form hypothesis, gather data, analyze, document findings) in writing, for both a 'confirmed hit' outcome and a 'clean, nothing found' outcome, and state what 'refine and repeat' looks like differently in each case.
slots.deliverable: Your written four-stage loop walkthrough for both outcomes (hit and clean), with a differing refine-and-repeat plan for each.

lessons.title: Hunting with MITRE ATT&CK as a Map

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one ATT&CK tactic other than Lateral Movement (e.g. Credential Access or Persistence), name two specific techniques under it with their T-numbers, and write a specific, testable hypothesis for each — following the lesson's T1021/RDP worked example — then describe what an ATT&CK Navigator heat map entry for each would look like if neither had ever been hunted.
slots.deliverable: Your written two-technique hypothesis set for your chosen tactic, plus your description of their unshaded heat-map status.

lessons.title: Turning a Successful Hunt into a Permanent Detection

slots.practicalActivity: Take your earlier hunt's confirmed-hit scenario and write out the specific Scheduled Analytics Rule settings (run frequency, a lookback window longer than that frequency, and alert threshold) you'd configure to convert that hunting query into a permanent rule, following the lesson's guidance on what changes between a one-off hunt and a scheduled rule.
slots.deliverable: Your written Scheduled Analytics Rule configuration (query, frequency, lookback, threshold) converting your hunt into a permanent detection.

lessons.title: Capstone Part 1: Detection Through Containment
lessons.chapterTitle: Job-Ready Capstone: Full Incident Response Exercise

slots.practicalActivity: Working through Alderbrook Wealth Partners' case, write your own triage checklist confirming Teresa Marsh's impossible-travel alert is real (VPN check, known-traveler check, device/MFA check), explain specifically what the investigation graph's Account-to-Host link surfaced that the original analytics rule never named, and write the evidence-safe containment sequence (capture, then isolate, then disable) in the correct order.
slots.deliverable: Your written triage checklist confirming the incident, your explanation of what the investigation graph surfaced beyond the original alert, and your evidence-safe containment sequence in order.

lessons.title: Capstone Part 2: Eradication, Recovery, and the Report
lessons.chapterTitle: Job-Ready Capstone: Full Incident Response Exercise

slots.practicalActivity: Working through WKSTN-FIN-14's forensic capture, write out why the disguised MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTaskMachineUA scheduled task justified a full rebuild from a verified-clean backup rather than live cleanup, write your own three-check validation plan (Defender scan, scheduled-task baseline comparison, tenant-wide forensic re-run) before the device returns to Teresa, and draft at least two of the after-action report's four follow-up items in the owner/deadline/outcome format.
slots.deliverable: Your written rebuild-vs-clean justification, your three-check validation plan, and at least two fully specified after-action-report follow-up items.

lessons.title: Capstone Part 3: The Hunt That Finds What Sentinel Missed
lessons.chapterTitle: Job-Ready Capstone: Full Incident Response Exercise

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the hypothesis-driven hunt's reasoning for why the team pivoted to inbox-forwarding-rule activity (T1114.003) instead of re-running Teresa's exact impossible-travel indicators, explain specifically why Daniel Oyelaran's compromised account never triggered the impossible-travel rule, and write the Scheduled Analytics Rule settings (hourly, entity-mapped to Account, severity High, T1114.003 tag) that convert this hunt into a permanent detection.
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation of the hunt's pivot reasoning and why the second account evaded the existing rule, plus your Scheduled Analytics Rule configuration for the new permanent detection.

lessons.title: Job-Ready Foundation Review and What's Next
lessons.chapterTitle: Job-Ready Capstone: Full Incident Response Exercise

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own chapter-by-chapter mapping of this course's eight chapters to specific moments in the Alderbrook Wealth Partners case, following the lesson's own structure, then answer the lesson's check-yourself question in writing: which of the six prerequisite courses would have been hardest to remove from the capstone's case, and what specifically would the SOC have gotten wrong without it?
slots.deliverable: Your written eight-chapter-to-case mapping, plus your answer naming the hardest-to-remove prerequisite course and the specific failure that would have resulted without it.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course — and the entire Job-Ready Foundation stage it closes out — a student can run a full, real incident response lifecycle end to end the way Alderbrook Wealth Partners' SOC actually did it: triage a fired analytics rule into a confirmed incident using VPN, known-traveler, and device/MFA checks; open the investigation graph to scope past the one entity an alert names and catch a second compromised asset (a laptop running a disguised remote-access tool) before it's missed; contain in an evidence-safe order — capture volatile forensic data, then isolate the host, then disable the account — rather than destroying what a later investigation will need; find an attacker's actual persistence mechanism in forensic data and decide, correctly, when a host needs a full rebuild from a verified-clean backup instead of live cleanup; validate a recovered system against concrete pass/fail criteria before it returns to production; write an after-action report with specific, owned, dated follow-up items instead of a narrative nobody acts on; and run a hypothesis-driven threat hunt, grounded in MITRE ATT&CK, that catches a second compromised account the SIEM never alerted on and converts that finding into a permanent detection rule. That is the specific, demonstrated toolkit of a Junior SOC Analyst or Cybersecurity Analyst — built across all seven courses of the Job-Ready Foundation stage and proven, in this capstone, on one real incident handled start to finish.
